title: Ἄρητος καὶ Ποδῆς
titleEn: The Deaths of Aretus and Podes — Iliad 17.481–581
part: The Deaths of Aretus and Podes (17.481–581)
about: Alcimedon takes the reins, and Hector, seeing Achilles’ immortal horses with weaker drivers, urges Aeneas to seize them; Chromius and Aretus go with them. Automedon prays, tells Alcimedon to keep the team close at his back, and calls the two Ajaxes and Menelaus to guard Patroclus’ body while he and Alcimedon face the attack. He kills Aretus, avoids Hector’s cast, and strips the body, boasting, once the Ajaxes have driven the Trojans back. Athena comes down from heaven at Zeus’ bidding, wrapped in a purple cloud and in Phoenix’s shape, and rouses Menelaus, who has prayed to her. He kills Podes, Hector’s friend, and drags the body away.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, Ἀλκιμέδων δὲ βοηθόον ἅρμ’ ἐπορούσας
καρπαλίμως μάστιγα καὶ ἡνία λάζετο χερσίν,
Αὐτομέδων δ’ ἀπόρουσε·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Alcimedon sprang up on the chariot that stood ready to help and quickly took the whip and the reins in his hands, while Automedon leapt down;
sentences.n: Automedon’s speech ended at 480, so this is narrative. ἐπορούσας ‘having rushed upon’ takes the chariot as its object. βοηθόον is from βοή ‘shout’ and θέω ‘run’, ‘running to a call’, so ‘aiding’, said of the chariot; the exact shade is not certain. λάζετο ‘took’ is the unaugmented aorist of λάζομαι, and ἀπόρουσε ‘leapt down’ is the aorist of ἀπορούω.

sentences.t:
νόησε δὲ φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ,
αὐτίκα δ’ Αἰνείαν προσεφώνεεν ἐγγὺς ἐόντα·
sentences.l:
and noticed it glorious Hector,
and at once to Aeneas he spoke, who was near:
sentences.i: and glorious Hector noticed it, and at once spoke to Aeneas, who was near him:
sentences.n: νόησε ‘noticed’ is unaugmented (Attic ἐνόησε), and its object is left unsaid: the chariot has changed hands. φαίδιμος ‘glorious’ is Hector’s stock epithet. αὐτίκα δ’ … προσεφώνεεν ἐγγὺς ἐόντα, ‘and at once spoke to …, who was near’, is a repeated line, always with a different name; προσεφώνεεν is the uncontracted imperfect of προσφωνέω ‘address’. A speech follows.

sentences.t:
Αἰνεία Τρώων βουληφόρε χαλκοχιτώνων
ἵππω τώδ’ ἐνόησα ποδώκεος Αἰακίδαο
ἐς πόλεμον προφανέντε σὺν ἡνιόχοισι κακοῖσι·
sentences.l:
“Aeneas, counsel-bearer of the bronze-shirted Trojans,
these two horses I noticed, of the fleet-footed descendant of Aeacus,
to war having come forth, with charioteers, base ones:
sentences.i: “Aeneas, counsellor of the bronze-shirted Trojans, I have noticed these two horses of the fleet-footed descendant of Aeacus, come forward into the war with poor charioteers;
sentences.n: Hector speaks. βουληφόρε ‘counsel-bearer’ is the vocative of the epithet; the same line stands at 5.180. ἵππω … προφανέντε are duals, ‘the two horses … having appeared’, and Αἰακίδαο is Achilles, ‘descendant of Aeacus’. ἐνόησα is the aorist ‘I noticed’. κακοῖσι ‘base’ of the charioteers means poor at the work, not wicked: Hector sees only Automedon and Alcimedon.
sentences.mark: Hector urges Aeneas to take the horses

sentences.t:
τώ κεν ἐελποίμην αἱρησέμεν, εἰ σύ γε θυμῷ
σῷ ἐθέλεις, ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἂν ἐφορμηθέντε γε νῶϊ
τλαῖεν ἐναντίβιον στάντες μαχέσασθαι Ἄρηϊ.
sentences.l:
Therefore I would hope to take them, if you, for your part, in your heart
wish it, since not, we two having rushed on them,
would they dare, standing, face to face to fight in war.”
sentences.i: So I would hope to take them, if you for your part are willing in your own heart, since once we two have rushed on them they would not dare to stand and fight us face to face in battle.”
sentences.n: τώ ‘so, then’ opens the consequence. ἐελποίμην is the optative of ἔλπομαι ‘hope’ with the epic doubled vowel, and αἱρησέμεν is the future infinitive of αἱρέω ‘take’. ἐφορμηθέντε is a dual participle agreeing with νῶϊ, ‘we two, having rushed on them’; the subject of τλαῖεν ‘would dare’ is the two charioteers, left unnamed. Ἄρηϊ is Ares standing for war, ‘in war’.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησεν ἐῢς πάϊς Ἀγχίσαο.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and did not disobey, the good son of Anchises.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the good son of Anchises did not disobey him.
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἀπίθησεν ‘and did not disobey’ is the stock way of saying that a command was obeyed. ἐῢς ‘good’ is the epic form of ἐύς, πάϊς is Attic παῖς ‘son’, and Ἀγχίσαο is the epic genitive of Ἀγχίσης (Attic -ου): Aeneas, named by his father.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ ἰθὺς βήτην βοέῃς εἰλυμένω ὤμους
αὔῃσι στερεῇσι· πολὺς δ’ ἐπελήλατο χαλκός.
sentences.l:
And the two went straight on, with oxhides wrapped about the shoulders,
dry and hard; and much bronze had been driven on.
sentences.i: The two went straight on, their shoulders wrapped in dry, hard oxhides; and much bronze had been hammered on.
sentences.n: τώ … βήτην is the dual ‘the two went’, Hector and Aeneas, as Chromius and Aretus follow in the next line. εἰλυμένω is a dual perfect participle of εἰλύω ‘wrap’, with ὤμους ‘at the shoulders’ an accusative of respect. βοέῃς is the epic dative plural of βοέη ‘oxhide’, and αὔῃσι the epic dative plural of αὖος ‘dry’. ἐπελήλατο is the pluperfect passive of ἐπελαύνω, here ‘drive on, hammer on’: bronze was worked onto the hides.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ ἅμα Χρομίος τε καὶ Ἄρητος θεοειδὴς
ἤϊσαν ἀμφότεροι·
sentences.l:
And with them together Chromius and Aretus, godlike in form,
were going, both of them;
sentences.i: With them went Chromius and Aretus, godlike in form, the pair of them;
sentences.n: τοῖσι ‘with them’ means Hector and Aeneas, and ἅμα ‘together with’ takes it. Χρομίος (Chromius) and Ἄρητος (Aretus) are Trojan fighters; the second is the one who dies at 17.517. θεοειδής is ‘godlike in form’ (εἶδος ‘form’). ἤϊσαν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’, and ἀμφότεροι is ‘both’.

sentences.t:
μάλα δέ σφισιν ἔλπετο θυμὸς
αὐτώ τε κτενέειν ἐλάαν τ’ ἐριαύχενας ἵππους
νήπιοι, οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔμελλον ἀναιμωτί γε νέεσθαι
αὖτις ἀπ’ Αὐτομέδοντος.
sentences.l:
and greatly for them hoped the heart
to kill the two themselves and to drive off the strong-necked horses,
foolish ones, and not were they going to return without bloodshed
again from Automedon.
sentences.i: and their hearts hoped greatly to kill the pair themselves and drive off the strong-necked horses; foolish as they were, they were not, after all, to come back from Automedon without bloodshed.
sentences.n: θυμός is singular, the ‘heart’ of the group. αὐτώ is the dual ‘the two themselves’ (Automedon and Alcimedon), κτενέειν the epic infinitive ‘to kill’, and ἐλάαν ‘to drive off’ (Attic ἐλαύνειν). ἐριαύχενας ‘strong-necked’ is the stock epithet of horses; the sense of ἐρι- is not known. νήπιοι is the poet’s comment, ‘foolish ones’. ἀναιμωτί is ‘without bloodshed’, from αἷμα ‘blood’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ εὐξάμενος Διὶ πατρὶ
ἀλκῆς καὶ σθένεος πλῆτο φρένας ἀμφὶ μελαίνας·
sentences.l:
And he, having prayed to father Zeus,
was filled with might and power about his dark wits;
sentences.i: And he, after praying to father Zeus, was filled with might and power about his dark wits;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is Automedon (ὁ as ‘he’). εὐξάμενος is the aorist middle participle of εὔχομαι, here ‘having prayed’. ἀλκῆς καὶ σθένεος ‘of might and of power’ are genitives with πλῆτο, ‘was filled’, the unaugmented aorist middle of πίμπλημι. φρένας ἀμφὶ μελαίνας ‘about his dark wits’ is a formula for the body’s seat of feeling; ἀμφί follows its noun.

sentences.t: αὐτίκα δ’ Ἀλκιμέδοντα προσηύδα πιστὸν ἑταῖρον·
sentences.l: and at once to Alcimedon he spoke, his trusty companion:
sentences.i: and at once spoke to Alcimedon, his trusty companion:
sentences.n: αὐτίκα δ’ … προσηύδα ‘and at once … spoke to’; Ἀλκιμέδοντα is the accusative of Ἀλκιμέδων. πιστὸν ἑταῖρον ‘trusty companion’ stands in apposition, as at 15.331. A speech follows.

sentences.t:
Ἀλκίμεδον μὴ δή μοι ἀπόπροθεν ἰσχέμεν ἵππους,
ἀλλὰ μάλ’ ἐμπνείοντε μεταφρένῳ·
sentences.l:
“Alcimedon, do not, now, for me far off hold the horses,
but very much breathing on my back;
sentences.i: “Alcimedon, do not hold the horses far from me, but keep them breathing right on my back;
sentences.n: Ἀλκίμεδον is the vocative (the name is Ἀλκιμέδων at 481). μὴ δή μοι … ἰσχέμεν is a prohibition with an infinitive, ‘do not hold’, the infinitive standing for an imperative; μοι is ‘from me’ and ἀπόπροθεν ‘far off’. ἐμπνείοντε is a dual participle for the two horses, ‘breathing on’, with μεταφρένῳ ‘on my back’ in the dative: he wants the team so close that he feels its breath.
sentences.mark: Automedon asks Alcimedon to keep close

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἔγωγε
Ἕκτορα Πριαμίδην μένεος σχήσεσθαι ὀΐω,
sentences.l:
for I, for my part,
think that Hector, Priam’s-son, will not hold back from his might,
sentences.i: for I do not think that Hector, son of Priam, will hold back from his might,
sentences.n: σχήσεσθαι is the future middle infinitive of ἔχω in the sense ‘restrain oneself’, and takes μένεος ‘from his might’ in the genitive. The negative οὐ belongs with that infinitive though it stands early, after γάρ: ‘I think he will not hold back’. Πριαμίδην is ‘son of Priam’, as Ἀτρεΐδης is ‘son of Atreus’. The sentence is finished by πρίν in the next line.

sentences.t:
πρίν γ’ ἐπ’ Ἀχιλλῆος καλλίτριχε βήμεναι ἵππω
νῶϊ κατακτείναντα, φοβῆσαί τε στίχας ἀνδρῶν
Ἀργείων, ἤ κ’ αὐτὸς ἐνὶ πρώτοισιν ἁλοίη.
sentences.l:
until at least onto the two fair-maned horses of Achilles he has stepped,
having killed us two, and put to flight the ranks of men,
Argives, or else himself among the foremost is caught.”
sentences.i: before he has mounted Achilles’ two fair-maned horses, after killing us two and routing the ranks of Argive men, or else is himself caught among the foremost.”
sentences.n: πρίν γ’ … βήμεναι ‘until he has stepped’ is πρίν with an infinitive after a negative main clause. βήμεναι is the epic infinitive of βαίνω (Attic βῆναι), and ἐπί takes the dual accusative ἵππω ‘onto the two horses’, καλλίτριχε being ‘fair-maned’. νῶϊ κατακτείναντα is an aorist participle in the accusative, Hector the subject: ‘having killed us two’. ἁλοίη is the aorist optative of ἁλίσκομαι ‘be caught’, with ἤ κε ‘or else’.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν Αἴαντε καλέσσατο καὶ Μενέλαον·
sentences.l: So having spoken, he called to him the two Ajaxes and Menelaus:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and called the two Ajaxes and Menelaus to him:
sentences.n: Αἴαντε is the dual of the name, ‘the two Ajaxes’, the Telamonian and the son of Oïleus. καλέσσατο is the aorist middle of καλέω, ‘called to himself’. The speaker is still Automedon, and another speech follows.

sentences.t:
Αἴαντ’ Ἀργείων ἡγήτορε καὶ Μενέλαε
ἤτοι μὲν τὸν νεκρὸν ἐπιτράπεθ’ οἵ περ ἄριστοι
ἀμφ’ αὐτῷ βεβάμεν καὶ ἀμύνεσθαι στίχας ἀνδρῶν,
νῶϊν δὲ ζωοῖσιν ἀμύνετε νηλεὲς ἦμαρ·
sentences.l:
“Ajaxes, two leaders of the Argives, and Menelaus,
the dead man indeed take in charge, you who are the best,
to stand about him and to ward off the ranks of men,
but for us two, the living, ward off the pitiless day;
sentences.i: “Ajaxes, you two leaders of the Argives, and Menelaus, take the dead man into your charge, you who are the best, to stand about him and ward off the ranks of men, and ward off the pitiless day for us two, who are alive;
sentences.n: Αἴαντ’ … ἡγήτορε is the dual vocative, and καὶ Μενέλαε adds Menelaus in the singular. ἤτοι μέν … νῶϊν δέ sets the Ajaxes’ task against his own. ἐπιτράπεθ’ is a middle imperative of ἐπιτρέπω; ‘take into your charge’ is a likely sense, not a sure one. βεβάμεν is the perfect infinitive of βαίνω ‘to stand’, and νῶϊν is the dual ‘for us two’. νηλεὲς ἦμαρ ‘pitiless day’ is death.
sentences.mark: Automedon calls the Ajaxes and Menelaus

sentences.t:
τῇδε γὰρ ἔβρισαν πόλεμον κάτα δακρυόεντα
Ἕκτωρ Αἰνείας θ’, οἳ Τρώων εἰσὶν ἄριστοι.
sentences.l:
For here have borne down, through the tearful war,
Hector and Aeneas, who of the Trojans are the best.
sentences.i: For here, all through the tearful war, Hector and Aeneas have borne down on us, they who are the best of the Trojans.
sentences.n: τῇδε is ‘here, on this side’. ἔβρισαν is the aorist of βρίθω ‘be heavy, press hard’, here ‘have borne down’, with no object stated. πόλεμον κάτα is κατὰ πόλεμον with the preposition after its noun, ‘throughout the war’. δακρυόεντα ‘tearful’ is the epithet of war. Αἰνείας θ’ joins Aeneas to Hector as subject.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἤτοι μὲν ταῦτα θεῶν ἐν γούνασι κεῖται·
ἥσω γὰρ καὶ ἐγώ, τὰ δέ κεν Διὶ πάντα μελήσει.
sentences.l:
But indeed these things lie on the knees of the gods;
for I too will hurl, and all the rest will be a care to Zeus.”
sentences.i: But these things lie on the knees of the gods; for I too will throw, and all the rest will be a care to Zeus.”
sentences.n: θεῶν ἐν γούνασι κεῖται ‘lies on the knees of the gods’ is the formula for leaving the outcome to heaven; the Greek verb is singular, as the plural ταῦτα takes a singular verb. ἥσω is the future of ἵημι ‘send, hurl’, said of the spear he is about to throw (516). τὰ δέ … πάντα is ‘and all the rest’, and μελήσει ‘will be a care’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα, καὶ ἀμπεπαλὼν προΐει δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος,
καὶ βάλεν Ἀρήτοιο κατ’ ἀσπίδα πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and having brandished it he sent forth his long-shadowed spear,
and hit Aretus on the shield, equal on every side;
sentences.i: So he said, and brandishing it he sent forth his long-shadowed spear, and hit Aretus on his shield, equal on every side;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα καί ‘so he said, and’ is the formula that closes a speech and starts the action; ἦ is the old ‘he said’. ἀμπεπαλών ‘brandishing’ is the aorist participle meaning ‘having swung back’ the spear, and προΐει is the imperfect of προΐημι ‘send forth’. δολιχόσκιον ‘long-shadowed’ is the stock epithet of the spear. Ἀρήτοιο is the epic genitive of Ἄρητος. πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην ‘equal on every side’ is the stock phrase for a round shield.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ οὐκ ἔγχος ἔρυτο, διὰ πρὸ δὲ εἴσατο χαλκός,
νειαίρῃ δ’ ἐν γαστρὶ διὰ ζωστῆρος ἔλασσεν.
sentences.l:
and it did not guard against the spear, but right through rushed the bronze,
and in the lower belly through the belt drove it.
sentences.i: but the shield did not keep the spear out: the bronze sped right through it, and he drove the spear through the belt into the lower belly.
sentences.n: ἣ is the shield (ἀσπίς, feminine), not a relative. ἔρυτο is the unaugmented aorist middle of ἐρύομαι ‘guard, ward off’, and διὰ πρὸ … εἴσατο ‘rushed right through’ is a stock phrase, εἴσατο being the aorist of ἵεμαι ‘speed’. ἔλασσεν is the aorist of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’. νειαίρῃ ‘lower’ is said of the belly. The spear passes through the shield and then the belt.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν ὀξὺν ἔχων πέλεκυν αἰζήϊος ἀνὴρ
κόψας ἐξόπιθεν κεράων βοὸς ἀγραύλοιο
ἶνα τάμῃ διὰ πᾶσαν, ὃ δὲ προθορὼν ἐρίπῃσιν,
sentences.l:
And as when, holding a sharp axe, a vigorous man,
having struck from behind the horns of a field-dwelling ox,
cuts through the whole sinew, and it, leaping forward, falls down,
sentences.i: And as when a vigorous man, holding a sharp axe, strikes from behind the horns of a field-dwelling ox and cuts through the whole sinew, and the ox springs forward and drops,
sentences.n: A comparison runs to 524. ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν takes the subjunctives τάμῃ ‘cuts’ and ἐρίπῃσιν ‘falls’, for a scene that happens again and again. αἰζήϊος ‘vigorous’ is said of a man in his prime; ἀγραύλοιο ‘field-dwelling’ is the stock epithet of cattle. ἶνα is ‘sinew’, here the neck’s as the picture requires, cut διὰ πᾶσαν ‘through all of it’. ὃ δέ ‘and it’ is the ox, and προθορών ‘leaping forward’ its last start.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ὅ γε προθορὼν πέσεν ὕπτιος· ἐν δέ οἱ ἔγχος
νηδυίοισι μάλ’ ὀξὺ κραδαινόμενον λύε γυῖα.
sentences.l:
so he, leaping forward, fell on his back; and in him the spear
in the bowels, very sharp, quivering, was loosening his limbs.
sentences.i: So Aretus leapt forward and fell on his back, and the spear, very sharp, quivering in his bowels, loosened his limbs.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρ’ ὅ γε completes the comparison: he is Aretus, springing forward as the ox does and falling. ὕπτιος is ‘on his back’. ἐν … νηδυίοισι is ‘in the bowels’ with ἐν split off (νηδύς ‘belly, bowels’; the dative plural is epic). κραδαινόμενον is the present passive participle of κραδαίνω ‘shake, quiver’, and λύε the unaugmented imperfect of λύω ‘loosen’. To loosen the limbs is the Homeric phrase for killing.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δ’ Αὐτομέδοντος ἀκόντισε δουρὶ φαεινῷ·
ἀλλ’ ὃ μὲν ἄντα ἰδὼν ἠλεύατο χάλκεον ἔγχος·
sentences.l:
And Hector at Automedon hurled with his shining spear;
but he, looking straight at it, avoided the bronze spear;
sentences.i: Hector hurled his shining spear at Automedon; but Automedon, seeing it coming straight at him, avoided the bronze spear;
sentences.n: ἀκόντισε ‘hurled’ (ἀκοντίζω, from ἄκων ‘javelin’) takes Αὐτομέδοντος in the genitive, ‘at Automedon’, and δουρὶ φαεινῷ is the dative ‘with a shining spear’. ἀλλ’ ὃ μέν ‘but he’ is Automedon. ἄντα ἰδών ‘looking straight at it’ says he saw it coming. ἠλεύατο is the unaugmented aorist of ἀλέομαι ‘avoid’.

sentences.t:
πρόσσω γὰρ κατέκυψε, τὸ δ’ ἐξόπιθεν δόρυ μακρὸν
οὔδει ἐνισκίμφθη, ἐπὶ δ’ οὐρίαχος πελεμίχθη
ἔγχεος·
sentences.i: for he bent forward, and the long spear behind him was fixed in the ground, and the butt-end of the spear shook;
sentences.n: The same lines stand at 16.611–612. πρόσσω … κατέκυψε ‘he bent forward’ is how Automedon avoided the spear. τὸ … δόρυ is ‘that spear’, which flew past him and stuck in the ground behind. ἐξόπιθεν is ‘from behind’, ἐνισκίμφθη ‘was fixed’, οὐρίαχος ‘butt-end’ (the spike at the foot of the shaft), and πελεμίχθη ‘was shaken’.

sentences.t: ἔνθα δ’ ἔπειτ’ ἀφίει μένος ὄβριμος Ἄρης.
sentences.l: and there then was letting go the might mighty Ares.
sentences.i: and then mighty Ares let the might go.
sentences.n: ἀφίει is the unaugmented imperfect of ἀφίημι ‘let go’. Whose might is not said: the spear’s force may be meant, or Ares, the war-god, may let his own might go. Both layers leave it open, as at 16.613, where the line stands too.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κε δὴ ξιφέεσσ’ αὐτοσχεδὸν ὁρμηθήτην
εἰ μή σφω’ Αἴαντε διέκριναν μεμαῶτε,
οἵ ῥ’ ἦλθον καθ’ ὅμιλον ἑταίρου κικλήσκοντος·
sentences.i: And now the two of them would have rushed at each other with swords at close quarters, if the two Ajaxes, in their eagerness, had not parted them, coming through the throng at the call of their companion;
sentences.n: This is contrary to fact: κε with the aorist ὁρμηθήτην ‘would have rushed’, a dual for Hector and Automedon, and σφω’ is the dual pronoun ‘the two of them’. εἰ μή … διέκριναν is ‘if they had not parted’. μεμαῶτε is a dual perfect participle, ‘eager’. αὐτοσχεδόν is ‘at close quarters’ and ξιφέεσσι ‘with swords’, with the epic -εσσι. ἑταίρου κικλήσκοντος is a genitive absolute, ‘their companion calling’.

sentences.t:
τοὺς ὑποταρβήσαντες ἐχώρησαν πάλιν αὖτις
Ἕκτωρ Αἰνείας τ’ ἠδὲ Χρομίος θεοειδής,
sentences.l:
Having shrunk in fear before them, drew back again
Hector and Aeneas and Chromius, godlike in form,
sentences.i: Hector and Aeneas and Chromius, godlike in form, shrank in fear before them and drew back again,
sentences.n: τούς ‘them’ are the two Ajaxes. ὑποταρβήσαντες is the aorist participle of ὑποταρβέω, ‘having shrunk in fear before’. ἐχώρησαν ‘drew back, gave way’ is the aorist of χωρέω, and πάλιν αὖτις ‘back again’ puts two words of the same meaning side by side. The subjects come last, in the second line; Aretus is not among them, as the next unit says.

sentences.t:
Ἄρητον δὲ κατ’ αὖθι λίπον δεδαϊγμένον ἦτορ
κείμενον·
sentences.l:
and Aretus they left right there, torn apart in the heart,
lying;
sentences.i: and they left Aretus lying right there, torn apart in the heart;
sentences.n: κατ’ αὖθι is ‘right there, on the spot’. λίπον is the unaugmented aorist of λείπω ‘leave’. δεδαϊγμένον is a perfect passive participle of δαΐζω ‘rend, tear apart’, and ἦτορ ‘heart’ is an accusative of respect, so ‘torn apart in the heart’. κείμενον ‘lying’ agrees with Ἄρητον.

sentences.t:
Αὐτομέδων δὲ θοῷ ἀτάλαντος Ἄρηϊ
τεύχεά τ’ ἐξενάριξε καὶ εὐχόμενος ἔπος ηὔδα·
sentences.l:
And Automedon, the equal of swift Ares,
despoiled the armour, and, declaring, spoke a word:
sentences.i: And Automedon, the equal of swift Ares, stripped off his armour and said, declaring aloud:
sentences.n: θοῷ ἀτάλαντος Ἄρηϊ ‘the equal of swift Ares’ is a stock comparison, with ἀτάλαντος taking the dative. ἐξενάριξε is the aorist of ἐξεναρίζω ‘strip a slain man’, from ἔναρα ‘spoils’, and τεύχεα are the dead man’s arms. εὐχόμενος here means ‘boasting, declaring aloud’, not ‘praying’. ἔπος ηὔδα ‘spoke a word’ is a formula, ηὔδα the imperfect of αὐδάω.

sentences.t:
ἦ δὴ μὰν ὀλίγον γε Μενοιτιάδαο θανόντος
κῆρ ἄχεος μεθέηκα χερείονά περ καταπέφνων.
sentences.l:
“Truly indeed a little, at least, with Menoetius’-son dead,
my heart from grief I have let go, though one lesser I killed.”
sentences.i: “Truly, I have eased my heart of its grief a little, at least, for the death of the son of Menoetius, though the man I killed was the lesser.”
sentences.n: ἦ δὴ μάν ‘truly indeed’ opens an emphatic claim, and ὀλίγον γε is ‘a little, at least’. Μενοιτιάδαο θανόντος is a genitive absolute, ‘with the son of Menoetius dead’, that is, Patroclus. μεθέηκα is an epic form of the aorist of μεθίημι ‘let go’; its object is κῆρ ‘heart’, and ἄχεος ‘from grief’ is a genitive of separation. χερείονα is ‘lesser, inferior’, and καταπέφνων a participle from the root of φόνος, ‘having killed’.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ἐς δίφρον ἑλὼν ἔναρα βροτόεντα
θῆκ’, ἂν δ’ αὐτὸς ἔβαινε πόδας καὶ χεῖρας ὕπερθεν
αἱματόεις ὥς τίς τε λέων κατὰ ταῦρον ἐδηδώς.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, into the chariot, taking the bloody spoils,
he put them, and himself went up, on feet and hands above,
bloody, like some lion that has eaten down a bull.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and taking the bloody spoils he put them in the chariot and climbed up himself, bloody on his feet and hands all over, like a lion that has devoured a bull.
sentences.n: ἂν δ’ is ἀνά separated from its verb, ‘up’ (ἂν … ἔβαινε, Attic ἀνέβαινε ‘climbed up’). πόδας καὶ χεῖρας are accusatives of respect with αἱματόεις ‘bloody’. ὕπερθεν ‘above, on top’ is hard to place, and ‘all over’ is the sense taken here. ὥς τίς τε λέων is ‘like some lion’, and κατὰ … ἐδηδώς is ‘having eaten down’, a perfect participle of ἔδω ‘eat’ with the preposition split off.

sentences.t:
ἂψ δ’ ἐπὶ Πατρόκλῳ τέτατο κρατερὴ ὑσμίνη
ἀργαλέη πολύδακρυς, ἔγειρε δὲ νεῖκος Ἀθήνη
οὐρανόθεν καταβᾶσα·
sentences.i: Again the strong battle was stretched over Patroclus, grievous and full of tears, and Athena, who had come down from heaven, stirred up the quarrel;
sentences.n: ἂψ ‘back again’ marks the fighting as resumed. τέτατο is the pluperfect passive of τείνω, ‘was stretched’, as of a rope drawn tight. πολύδακρυς ‘of many tears’ is a by-form of πολυδάκρυος (see 17.192). ἔγειρε ‘was rousing’ is the imperfect of ἐγείρω, and νεῖκος is the strife of battle, rendered ‘quarrel’ as in the table. οὐρανόθεν ‘from heaven’ goes with καταβᾶσα, the aorist participle ‘having come down’.

sentences.t:
προῆκε γὰρ εὐρύοπα Ζεὺς
ὀρνύμεναι Δαναούς· δὴ γὰρ νόος ἐτράπετ’ αὐτοῦ.
sentences.l:
for had sent her far-thundering Zeus
to rouse the Danaans; for now his mind had turned.
sentences.i: for far-thundering Zeus had sent her to rouse the Danaans; for his mind had now turned.
sentences.n: προῆκε ‘had sent’ is the aorist of προΐημι, and its object, Athena, is not stated. εὐρύοπα is the stock epithet ‘far-thundering’; its meaning is disputed (‘far-sounding’ and ‘far-seeing’ are the other proposals). ὀρνύμεναι is the epic infinitive of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’. The last clause says that Zeus’ mind ἐτράπετο ‘had turned’ (aorist middle of τρέπω); to what it turned is not said, but the sense is a change of purpose in the Danaans’ favour.

sentences.t:
ἠΰτε πορφυρέην ἶριν θνητοῖσι τανύσσῃ
Ζεὺς ἐξ οὐρανόθεν τέρας ἔμμεναι ἢ πολέμοιο
ἢ καὶ χειμῶνος δυσθαλπέος, ὅς ῥά τε ἔργων
ἀνθρώπους ἀνέπαυσεν ἐπὶ χθονί, μῆλα δὲ κήδει,
sentences.l:
As when a purple rainbow for mortals stretches
Zeus from heaven, to be a portent either of war
or of winter hard to warm, which from their works
men has made to rest upon the earth, and the flocks distresses,
sentences.i: As when Zeus stretches a purple rainbow from heaven for mortals, to be a portent either of war or of a winter hard to warm, which makes men rest from their work upon the earth, and distresses the flocks,
sentences.n: ἠΰτε ‘as when’ takes the subjunctive τανύσσῃ ‘stretches out’. ἶριν is the rainbow, the common noun that is also the goddess’ name. τέρας ἔμμεναι is ‘to be a portent’, ἔμμεναι being the epic infinitive of εἰμί. χειμῶνος δυσθαλπέος is ‘a winter hard to warm’, that is, bitterly cold, and ὅς refers back to it. ἀνέπαυσεν is a general aorist, ‘makes … rest’; κήδει is ‘distresses’ (κήδω), and μῆλα are sheep and goats.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἣ πορφυρέῃ νεφέλῃ πυκάσασα ἓ αὐτὴν
δύσετ’ Ἀχαιῶν ἔθνος, ἔγειρε δὲ φῶτα ἕκαστον.
sentences.l:
so she, in a purple cloud having wrapped herself,
entered the band of the Achaeans, and was rousing each man.
sentences.i: so she, wrapping herself in a purple cloud, entered the band of the Achaeans and roused each man.
sentences.n: ὣς closes the comparison, and ἣ is ‘she’, Athena. πυκάσασα ἓ αὐτήν is ‘having covered herself’: πυκάζω is ‘cover thickly’, ἕ the epic reflexive, and αὐτήν ‘herself’. δύσετο is the unaugmented aorist middle of δύω ‘enter’. ἔθνος is ‘band’, a body of people, as the table has it. φῶτα is the accusative of φώς ‘man’, and ἔγειρε ‘was rousing’ is the same verb as in 544.

sentences.t:
πρῶτον δ’ Ἀτρέος υἱὸν ἐποτρύνουσα προσηύδα
ἴφθιμον Μενέλαον·
sentences.l:
And first the son of Atreus, urging him on, she spoke to,
mighty Menelaus;
sentences.i: And first she spoke to the son of Atreus, urging him on, mighty Menelaus;
sentences.n: Athena is still the subject, as the next lines make plain. Ἀτρέος υἱόν ‘son of Atreus’ is Menelaus, and ἴφθιμον ‘mighty’ is the epithet, set in apposition after the verb. ἐποτρύνουσα is ‘urging on’ (ἐποτρύνω), and προσηύδα ‘she spoke to’, as at 500. Why she chose Menelaus first the next unit says: he was close by.

sentences.t:
ὃ γάρ ῥά οἱ ἐγγύθεν ἦεν·
εἰσαμένη Φοίνικι δέμας καὶ ἀτειρέα φωνήν·
sentences.l:
for he was near to her;
making herself like Phoenix in body and in unwearied voice:
sentences.i: for he was close by her; taking the likeness of Phoenix in body and in her unwearied voice:
sentences.n: ὃ γάρ ῥά οἱ: ὃ ‘he’ is Menelaus and οἱ ‘to her’; ἐγγύθεν ἦεν ‘was close by’. εἰσαμένη is the aorist participle of εἴδομαι, ‘making herself like’, a goddess taking a mortal’s shape; Φοίνικι is the old Phoenix, Achilles’ tutor, not a Phoenician. δέμας and φωνήν are accusatives of respect, ‘in body and voice’, and ἀτειρέα ‘unwearied’ is a voice that does not tire.

sentences.t:
σοὶ μὲν δὴ Μενέλαε κατηφείη καὶ ὄνειδος
ἔσσεται εἴ κ’ Ἀχιλῆος ἀγαυοῦ πιστὸν ἑταῖρον
τείχει ὕπο Τρώων ταχέες κύνες ἑλκήσουσιν.
sentences.l:
“For you indeed, Menelaus, a shame and a reproach
will there be, if of Achilles, the noble, the trusty companion
under the wall the swift dogs of the Trojans shall drag.
sentences.i: “For you, Menelaus, it will be a shame and a reproach if the swift dogs of the Trojans drag the trusty companion of noble Achilles under the wall.
sentences.n: Athena, as Phoenix, speaks. σοὶ μὲν δή ‘for you indeed’ puts the shame on Menelaus himself. κατηφείη καὶ ὄνειδος ‘a shame and a reproach’ is a pair (κατηφείη from κατηφής ‘downcast’). εἰ κε with the future ἑλκήσουσιν ‘if … shall drag’ is a vivid condition. Ἀχιλῆος ἀγαυοῦ is ‘noble Achilles’, and πιστὸν ἑταῖρον ‘trusty companion’ is Patroclus. τείχει ὕπο is ὑπὸ τείχει, ‘under the wall’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἔχεο κρατερῶς, ὄτρυνε δὲ λαὸν ἅπαντα.
sentences.l: But hold yourself strongly, and urge on the people, all of it.”
sentences.i: But hold on strongly, and urge on the whole army.”
sentences.n: ἔχεο is the middle imperative of ἔχω, ‘hold yourself’, that is, hold firm, and κρατερῶς is ‘strongly’. ὄτρυνε is the aorist imperative of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, and λαὸν ἅπαντα ‘the people, all of it’ is the whole army. The same line stands at 16.501. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος·
sentences.l: Her then in turn addressed Menelaus, good at the war-cry:
sentences.i: Then Menelaus, good at the war-cry, spoke to her in turn:
sentences.n: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε ‘and her in turn he addressed’ is the stock reply formula. τήν is feminine, the narrator’s view: Menelaus takes the speaker for Phoenix, but the poet knows it is Athena. προσέειπε is the aorist of προσεῖπον ‘address’, and βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ is Menelaus’ stock epithet.

sentences.t:
Φοῖνιξ ἄττα γεραιὲ παλαιγενές, εἰ γὰρ Ἀθήνη
δοίη κάρτος ἐμοί, βελέων δ’ ἀπερύκοι ἐρωήν·
sentences.l:
“Phoenix, father, aged one, of ancient birth, if only Athena
would give strength to me, and keep off the rush of shafts;
sentences.i: “Father Phoenix, aged one, of great age, if only Athena would give me strength and keep off the force of the shafts;
sentences.n: Menelaus speaks, thinking he addresses Phoenix. ἄττα ‘father’ is a title for an older man, γεραιέ ‘aged one’, and παλαιγενές ‘of ancient birth’; the address is that of 9.607 with a different last word. εἰ γάρ with the optatives δοίη and ἀπερύκοι is a wish, ‘if only … would give … and keep off’. κάρτος is ‘strength’, and βελέων ἐρωήν ‘the rush of the shafts’ is the onrush of missiles.

sentences.t:
τώ κεν ἔγωγ’ ἐθέλοιμι παρεστάμεναι καὶ ἀμύνειν
Πατρόκλῳ· μάλα γάρ με θανὼν ἐσεμάσσατο θυμόν.
sentences.l:
then I, for my part, would be willing to stand by and ward off
for Patroclus; for greatly, dead, he touched me in my heart;
sentences.i: then I for my part would be willing to stand by and defend Patroclus; for dead as he is, he has greatly touched my heart;
sentences.n: τώ κεν is ‘then’, with ἐθέλοιμι ‘I would be willing’. παρεστάμεναι is the epic infinitive of παρίστημι ‘stand by’, and ἀμύνειν with the dative Πατρόκλῳ is ‘ward off harm for’, that is, defend. ἐσεμάσσατο is the aorist middle of a rare verb ‘touch’ with the prefix ἐς-; ‘touched my heart’ is taken as ‘moved me’. θανών ‘dead’ and θυμόν ‘heart’ (an accusative of respect) complete it.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ Ἕκτωρ πυρὸς αἰνὸν ἔχει μένος, οὐδ’ ἀπολήγει
χαλκῷ δηϊόων· τῷ γὰρ Ζεὺς κῦδος ὀπάζει.
sentences.l:
But Hector has the fearsome might of fire, and does not cease
cutting down with bronze; for to him Zeus grants glory.”
sentences.i: But Hector has a fearsome might like fire, and does not stop cutting men down with bronze; for Zeus grants him glory.”
sentences.n: πυρὸς … μένος ‘the might of fire’ likens Hector’s fury to fire, and αἰνόν is ‘fearsome’. ἀπολήγει ‘ceases’ takes a participle, δηϊόων ‘cutting down’, from δηϊόω ‘hew, slay’, with χαλκῷ ‘with bronze’. τῷ … Ζεὺς κῦδος ὀπάζει is ‘Zeus grants glory to him’ (ὀπάζω ‘make follow, grant’), and the clause says why Hector cannot be stopped. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, γήθησεν δὲ θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη,
ὅττί ῥά οἱ πάμπρωτα θεῶν ἠρήσατο πάντων.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and rejoiced the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena,
because to her first of all the gods he had prayed.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, rejoiced, because he had prayed to her first of all the gods.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο, γήθησεν δέ ‘so he spoke, and … rejoiced’ is the formula for pleasure at a speech. ὅττι is epic for ὅτι ‘because’, and ῥά adds ‘as it turned out’. οἱ is ‘to her’, Athena. πάμπρωτα ‘first of all’ governs θεῶν πάντων ‘of all the gods’, and ἠρήσατο is the aorist of ἀράομαι ‘pray’. Menelaus has prayed to her, as a man in need.

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ βίην ὤμοισι καὶ ἐν γούνεσσιν ἔθηκε,
καί οἱ μυίης θάρσος ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἐνῆκεν,
ἥ τε καὶ ἐργομένη μάλα περ χροὸς ἀνδρομέοιο
ἰσχανάᾳ δακέειν, λαρόν τέ οἱ αἷμ’ ἀνθρώπου·
sentences.l:
And in his shoulders and in his knees she set might,
and the boldness of a fly in his chest she put,
which, even when kept off very much from a man’s skin,
is eager to bite, and to it the blood of a man is sweet;
sentences.i: She set might in his shoulders and his knees, and put into his chest the boldness of a fly, which, however often it is driven off from a man’s skin, is bent on biting, for the blood of a man is sweet to it;
sentences.n: ἔθηκε ‘set’ and ἐνῆκεν ‘put in’ have Athena as subject; ἐν … ἔθηκε is split. μυίης is the epic genitive of μυῖα ‘fly’, and the comparison is its stubbornness. ἐργομένη is the passive participle of εἴργω ‘keep off’. ἰσχανάᾳ δακέειν: the usual ἰσχανάω is ‘hold back’, but with an infinitive it seems to mean ‘be eager, bent on’ to bite; the shade is not certain. λαρόν ‘sweet, pleasant to the taste’ goes with αἷμα.

sentences.t:
τοίου μιν θάρσευς πλῆσε φρένας ἀμφὶ μελαίνας,
βῆ δ’ ἐπὶ Πατρόκλῳ, καὶ ἀκόντισε δουρὶ φαεινῷ.
sentences.l:
With such boldness she filled him, about his dark wits,
and he went to Patroclus, and hurled with his shining spear.
sentences.i: She filled him, about his dark wits, with such boldness; and he went to Patroclus and hurled his shining spear.
sentences.n: μιν is Menelaus. τοίου … θάρσευς is the epic genitive of θάρσος ‘boldness’, the genitive of what fills him, ‘with such boldness’, answering the fly. πλῆσε is the unaugmented aorist of πίμπλημι ‘fill’; φρένας ἀμφὶ μελαίνας is the formula of 499. ἐπὶ Πατρόκλῳ with the dative means ‘at, over’ the body. ἀκόντισε ‘hurled’, with δουρὶ φαεινῷ ‘shining spear’, has no stated target; the next lines name it.

sentences.t:
ἔσκε δ’ ἐνὶ Τρώεσσι Ποδῆς υἱὸς Ἠετίωνος
ἀφνειός τ’ ἀγαθός τε·
sentences.l:
And there was among the Trojans Podes, son of Eetion,
rich and good;
sentences.i: There was among the Trojans Podes, the son of Eetion, a rich and good man;
sentences.n: ἔσκε is the iterative form of εἰμί, here simply ‘there was’, the formula that brings in a minor figure; Τρώεσσι is the epic dative plural. Ποδῆς (Podes) is new in the poem. Ἠετίων (Eetion) is also the name of Andromache’s father, and the text does not say whether this is the same man. ἀφνειός ‘rich’ and ἀγαθός ‘good’ are set side by side with τε … τε.

sentences.t:
μάλιστα δέ μιν τίεν Ἕκτωρ
δήμου, ἐπεί οἱ ἑταῖρος ἔην φίλος εἰλαπιναστής·
sentences.l:
and most of all him honoured Hector
of the people, since to him a companion he was, dear, a banqueter;
sentences.i: and Hector honoured him most of all the people, since he was his dear companion at the feast;
sentences.n: τίεν is the unaugmented imperfect of τίω ‘honour’, so ‘used to honour’. μάλιστα … δήμου is a partitive genitive, ‘most of the people’, δῆμος being the townsfolk. ἔην is the epic imperfect of εἰμί. εἰλαπιναστής is a rare word from εἰλαπίνη ‘feast’, ‘one who joins in feasts’, a banqueter, so ‘companion at the feast’.

sentences.t:
τόν ῥα κατὰ ζωστῆρα βάλε ξανθὸς Μενέλαος
ἀΐξαντα φόβον δέ, διὰ πρὸ δὲ χαλκὸν ἔλασσε·
sentences.l:
Him then at the belt hit fair-haired Menelaus,
as he darted off to flight, and right through drove the bronze;
sentences.i: Fair-haired Menelaus hit him at the belt as he darted off to flight, and drove the bronze right through him;
sentences.n: τόν ῥα … βάλε ‘hit him then’ opens the line; κατὰ ζωστῆρα is ‘at the belt’. ἀΐξαντα is the aorist participle of ἀΐσσω ‘dart’. φόβον δέ is the edition’s spelling of φόβονδε ‘towards flight’; φόβος in battle is ‘flight’, not ‘fear’. διὰ πρὸ δέ ‘right through’ goes with χαλκὸν ἔλασσε ‘drove the bronze’, ἔλασσε being the aorist of ἐλαύνω.

sentences.t:
δούπησεν δὲ πεσών· ἀτὰρ Ἀτρεΐδης Μενέλαος
νεκρὸν ὑπ’ ἐκ Τρώων ἔρυσεν μετὰ ἔθνος ἑταίρων.
sentences.l:
and he fell with a thud; but the son of Atreus, Menelaus,
the corpse out from under the Trojans drew to the company of his companions.
sentences.i: and he fell with a thud; and Menelaus, son of Atreus, drew the corpse out from the Trojans to the company of his companions.
sentences.n: δούπησεν δὲ πεσών ‘and he fell with a thud’ is a stock line for a man’s fall, δοῦπος being the thud. ἀτάρ is ‘but, and’. νεκρόν is the body of Podes, whom Menelaus has just killed. ὑπ’ ἐκ is two prepositions together, ‘out from under’, with Τρώων. ἔρυσεν is the aorist of ἐρύω ‘drag’, and μετὰ ἔθνος ἑταίρων is ‘to the company of his companions’.
